module_title: UNSC Chapter VII Powers, Treaty Invalidity & ICJ Climate Opinion
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams, UGC NET, and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the coercive powers of the Security Council, the strict grounds for terminating a treaty, and the 2025/2026 ICJ Advisory Opinion that has reshaped international environmental law.

core_concepts.title: UNSC Powers under Chapter VII
core_concepts.description:
Chapter VII of the UN Charter grants the Security Council the power to maintain or restore international peace.
- Article 39: The UNSC determines the existence of any threat to the peace, breach of the peace, or act of aggression.
- Article 41 (Non-Military): Power to impose binding economic sanctions, arms embargoes, and sever diplomatic relations.
- Article 42 (Military): Power to authorize the use of armed force by air, sea, or land forces as necessary to restore peace (The legal basis for UN peacekeeping and authorized military interventions).

core_concepts.title: Invalidity and Termination of Treaties (VCLT)
core_concepts.description:
How does a binding treaty die?
1. Material Breach (Art 60): If State A fundamentally violates the treaty, State B can invoke the breach as a ground for terminating the treaty.
2. Rebus sic stantibus (Art 62 - Fundamental Change of Circumstances): A treaty can be terminated if there is an unforeseeable, fundamental change in the circumstances that existed at the time of signing, AND the existence of those circumstances was an essential basis of the consent to be bound. 
3. Supervening Impossibility of Performance (Art 61): The permanent destruction or disappearance of an object indispensable for the execution of the treaty (e.g., an island sinks).

core_concepts.title: The 2025 ICJ Advisory Opinion on Climate Change
core_concepts.description:
A historic development reshaping international liability.
- The Event: On July 23, 2025, the ICJ delivered a landmark Advisory Opinion regarding the obligations of States in respect of climate change. 
- Legal Impact: The Court confirmed that the law of State responsibility applies if States fail to fulfill their environmental obligations, opening a pathway for establishing causation of harm and reparations. 
- The 2026 Follow-up: In late May 2026, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution operationalizing this ICJ opinion, significantly empowering small island states to initiate future climate litigation and pursue accountability for environmental damage.

core_concepts.title: Jus Cogens and Treaty Invalidity (Article 53 & 64 VCLT)
core_concepts.description:
- Article 53: A treaty is void *ab initio* (from the start) if, at the time of its conclusion, it conflicts with a peremptory norm of general international law (*Jus Cogens*).
- Article 64: If a *new* peremptory norm of general international law emerges, any existing treaty which is in conflict with that new norm becomes void and terminates.

important_entities.name: Article 51: The Right of Self-Defense
important_entities.key_fact: The exception to the prohibition on the use of force.
important_entities.significance: Article 2(4) of the UN Charter prohibits the use of force. Article 51 is the sole exception (aside from UNSC authorization). It grants states the inherent right of individual or collective self-defense if an 'armed attack' occurs, but ONLY until the Security Council has taken measures to maintain peace.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The 'Rebus sic stantibus Political Change' Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Can a state invoke *Rebus sic stantibus* (Fundamental Change of Circumstances) just because a new political party comes to power or a policy becomes financially burdensome? **NO**. The ICJ applies this doctrine extremely restrictively (e.g., *Gabcikovo-Nagymaros Case*). A mere change in government policy or economic difficulty does NOT legally justify terminating a treaty.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The logical sequence of the Security Council's coercive powers: identify the threat (39), apply non-military pressure (41), and use military force if necessary (42).

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains, when discussing international climate accountability, you must integrate the **July 2025 ICJ Advisory Opinion** and the **May 2026 UNGA Resolution**, demonstrating how 'soft law' advisory opinions crystallize into actionable global norms [1.1.1].
